questions.text: Burking involves which combination of asphyxial mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Burking (the Burke and Hare method) combines simultaneous chest compression (traumatic asphyxia) with covering the mouth/nose (smothering), causing rapid death from combined asphyxial mechanisms without leaving obvious external marks.

questions.text: What is the most common cause of inward (central) hyoid bone fracture?
questions.explanation: Throttling involves direct manual compression of the neck, characteristically producing an inward/central hyoid bone fracture, distinguishing it from hanging or ligature strangulation.

questions.text: Which method of asphyxia shows the MOST severe internal neck damage?
questions.explanation: In throttling, the hands directly grip and compress the neck with intense, sustained pressure, causing tears in the sternomastoid muscle, hyoid fracture, thyroid cartilage fractures, and even cervical spine injury — more severe than the mechanisms in hanging or ligature strangulation.

questions.text: The neck shows extensive laceration, tears in the sternomastoid, and fracture-dislocation of C2-C3 vertebrae. These findings are most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Judicial (long-drop) hanging involves a measured drop generating massive kinetic energy, producing a hangman's fracture (C2-C3 fracture-ddislocation and sternomastoid tearing from cervical spinal cord disruption — findings not typically seen in the shorter drops of suicidal or accidental hanging.

questions.text: What are the characteristic features of a ligature mark in strangulation?
questions.explanation: Ligature strangulation produces a horizontal (level), low (below the thyroid cartilage), and complete (fully encircling) mark, in contrast to hanging's characteristically oblique, high, and incomplete mark.

questions.text: Which features characterize ligature marks in strangulation?
options: Associated with multiple lines on the neck at varying heights
Marks positioned high on the neck
originalOptions: Associated with multiple lines on the neck at varying heights
Marks positioned high on the neck
questions.explanation: Ligature strangulation produces transverse (horizontal), complete, low-neck marks, distinct from the oblique, high, often incomplete marks of hanging.

questions.text: Abrasions found on the neck are always considered what until proven otherwise?
questions.explanation: Neck abrasions (from fingernails or a ligature) are presumed indicative of strangulation until proven otherwise — a key medicolegal principle guiding initial death investigation.

questions.text: What are the characteristics of the frothy secretions seen in drowning?
questions.explanation: Drowning froth is classically white, fine, persistent, leathery, and tenacious — not bloody or turbid unless there is additional injury.

questions.text: In drowning, which finding is most indicative of the time passed since death (time in water)?
questions.explanation: Washerwoman skin (macerated, wrinkled skin from prolonged water immersion) progresses in a time-dependent manner, making it the most reliable indicator of how long a body has been submerged.

questions.text: What finding is characteristic of traumatic asphyxia?
questions.explanation: In traumatic asphyxia, chest compression prevents venous return from the head, producing cyanosis above the compression site and pallor below it, creating a sharp line of demarcation.

questions.text: A clear line of demarcation on the body is always seen in which condition?
questions.explanation: Traumatic (compressive) asphyxia produces a sharp line of demarcation between the congested, cyanotic upper body and the relatively normal-appearing lower body, a finding not characteristic of hanging, gagging, or drowning.

questions.text: Petechial hemorrhages are typically seen in which condition?
questions.explanation: Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu spots) are a hallmark of asphyxia, especially traumatic/crush asphyxia, resulting from increased venous pressure rupturing capillaries in the face, conjunctivae, and skin above the compression site.

questions.text: What are the mechanisms of death in mechanical asphyxia?
options: Anoxia, pulmonary edema, vagal inhibition (reflex cardiac arrest), and cerebral ischemia
originalOptions: Anoxia, pulmonary edema, vagal inhibition (reflex cardiac arrest), and cerebral ischemia
questions.correctAnswer: B) Anoxia, pulmonary edema, vagal inhibition (reflex cardiac arrest), and cerebral ischemia
questions.correctAnswerText: Anoxia, pulmonary edema, vagal inhibition (reflex cardiac arrest), and cerebral ischemia
questions.explanation: Mechanical asphyxia causes death through multiple overlapping mechanisms: oxygen deprivation, pulmonary edema, vagal reflex cardiac arrest (especially relevant in hanging/strangulation), and cerebral hypoxia.

questions.text: Mechanical asphyxia is a type of:
questions.explanation: Mechanical asphyxia (hanging, drowning, smothering) prevents oxygen from entering the lungs, representing anoxic anoxia — failure of oxygen to reach the blood — rather than a defect in oxygen transport or cellular utilization.

questions.text: Death in an environment with decreased atmospheric oxygen levels (e.g., high altitude, enclosed spaces) results in what type of anoxia?
questions.explanation: Decreased inspired oxygen concentration directly causes anoxic (hypoxic) anoxia, since insufficient oxygen is available in the air to be taken up by the blood.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT part of the classic triad features of asphyxia?
options: Fluid in the left side of the heart
Petechial hemorrhages in skin of face and eyes
originalOptions: Fluid in the left side of the heart
Petechial hemorrhages in skin of face and eyes
questions.correctAnswer: B) Fluid in the left side of the heart
questions.correctAnswerText: Fluid in the left side of the heart
questions.explanation: The asphyxia triad consists of cyanosis, congestion, and petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu spots); fluid accumulation in the left heart is not a recognized feature — right heart dilatation is more typically associated with asphyxial death.

questions.text: How are antemortem hangings diagnosed?
options: By the presence of cadaveric spasm
By vital reaction signs (hemorrhage in ligature mark, skin abrasion)
originalOptions: By the presence of cadaveric spasm
By vital reaction signs (hemorrhage in ligature mark, skin abrasion)
questions.correctAnswer: B) By vital reaction signs (hemorrhage in ligature mark, skin abrasion)
questions.correctAnswerText: By vital reaction signs (hemorrhage in ligature mark, skin abrasion)
questions.explanation: Antemortem hanging is confirmed by vital reactions in the ligature mark — hemorrhage, WBC infiltration, and early tissue repair — which are absent when the ligature is applied postmortem.

questions.text: What is a sign of antemortem hanging?
questions.explanation: Dripping or dribbling of saliva from the angle of the mouth toward the shoulder is a vital sign requiring intact salivary gland function, confirming the person was alive during the hanging (antemortem).

questions.text: Hypostasis (livor mortis) in the lower limbs is a sign of which condition?
questions.explanation: In complete hanging, the body is fully suspended, causing blood to gravitate and pool in the lower limbs, producing lower-limb hypostasis.

questions.text: Abrasions around the mouth indicate which mechanism of asphyxia?
questions.explanation: Perioral abrasions from hand or pillow pressure applied to obstruct the airway are characteristic of smothering, distinguishing it from neck-focused mechanisms like throttling or hanging.

questions.text: What is the most common manner of death in choking?
questions.explanation: Choking from foreign body airway obstruction (food, small objects) is most commonly accidental; homicidal choking (e.g., forced feeding) is rare.

questions.text: Histotoxic anoxia is caused by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Cyanide inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (mitochondrial Complex IV), preventing cells from utilizing oxygen even when it is available in the blood — defining histotoxic (cellular) anoxia, unlike CO (which impairs oxygen transport) or CNS depressants.

questions.text: Complete hanging (as opposed to incomplete) is defined by which factor?
questions.explanation: Complete versus incomplete hanging is distinguished by whether the body is fully suspended off the ground or partially supported/touching a surface, not by the victim's physical characteristics.

questions.text: A 65-year-old found dead in seawater shows goose skin appearance, easily removable hair, and the right hand forcefully grasping grass weeds. This is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Forceful grasping of an object (weeds) at the instant of death represents cadaveric spasm — instantaneous muscle locking that proves the person was alive and gripping at the moment they entered the water, distinct from the gradual onset of ordinary rigor mortis.

questions.text: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) causes death via what type of anoxia?
options: Anoxic anoxia (respiratory muscle paralysis prevents air entry)
originalOptions: Anoxic anoxia (respiratory muscle paralysis prevents air entry)
questions.correctAnswer: A) Anoxic anoxia (respiratory muscle paralysis prevents air entry)
questions.correctAnswerText: Anoxic anoxia (respiratory muscle paralysis prevents air entry)
questions.explanation: GBS causes ascending paralysis leading to respiratory muscle failure, preventing adequate ventilation so oxygen cannot enter the lungs — anoxic anoxia, despite normal oxygen availability in the environment.

questions.text: What type of anoxia is caused by cyanide (HCN) poisoning?
questions.explanation: HCN inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (mitochondrial Complex IV), blocking cellular oxygen utilization despite normal oxygen delivery — defining histotoxic (cellular) anoxia.

questions.text: The vagus nerve shares the same anatomical root and exit point with which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: CN IX (glossopharyngeal) and CN X (vagus) both arise from the medulla oblongata and exit the skull together through the jugular foramen, making their close anatomical relationship medicolegally relevant to vagal reflex death in asphyxia
